podcast.title: "Lady Bo" Nickname and Relationship with Bo Diddley
podcast.body: Peggy Jones earned the nickname "Lady Bo" due to her close musical partnership with Bo Diddley, which led many to mistakenly assume they were a couple. In reality, she was married to the band's bass player. "Peggy was also known as Lady Bo because she and Bo were so tight that everybody just assumed that they were a couple. Not true. She was actually married to the band's bass player."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Departure for The Jewels
podcast.body: Peggy Jones contributed to many Bo Diddley records until approximately 1961, when she left the band to dedicate her time to her own group, The Jewels. "Peggy ended up on a lot of Bo Didley records until about 1961 before she left a spend time with her own band called The Jewels."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: One of the First Female Rock Guitarists
podcast.body: Peggy Jones joined Bo Diddley's band as a guitarist in 1957 and is recognized as one of the first female rock guitarists in a famous rock band. She later became known for her experimental use of guitar synthesizers, a rare application in R&B music at the time. "This Black woman was recognized as one of the first female rock guitarists in a famous rock band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pioneer of Guitar Synthesizers in R&B
podcast.body: Peggy Jones distinguished herself through her experiments with guitar synthesizers, which was an uncommon practice in R&B music when she was using them. This innovative approach highlighted her forward-thinking musicality beyond her role as a pioneering female rock guitarist. "She'd later be recognized for her experiments with guitar synthesizers and nobody used those in R&B music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pioneering Female Electric Guitarist in Rock
podcast.body: Peggy Jones, also known as Lady Bo, joined Bo Diddley's band in 1957 as a rhythm guitarist, potentially making her the first woman to be visibly playing electric guitar in a rock band. Her recruitment came after Diddley observed her carrying a guitar case. "And as such, she might have very well been the first woman to be visible as an electric guitarist in a rock band. This was 1957."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
